title: Toward a Bipartisan Rejection of Slopulism
author: @ByrneHobart
text:
In this issue:Toward a Bipartisan Rejection of Slopulism—It's gotten increasingly popular to frame economic issues in terms of a visible enemy—billionaires or foreigners, typically, though there's room for creativity and specificity for both—rather than in terms of tradeoffs. But the tradeoffs are real. It's time for politicians to start treating voters like adults.Super-Voting Org Charts—Jensen's back! And Nvidia's board would like you to know that it wasn't entirely their call.Sanctions and Supply Chains—IP leakage looks for the most porous boundary between rival countries.Liquidity—Pitching a blue-chip neocloud.Targeted Tariffs—Smarter tariffs.Political Pull—Mar-a-Lago can't recapture the heady days of 2025.The Diff November 23rd 20260:00/19:38Talk to this post on Read.Haus.Today's issue of The Diff is brought to you by our sponsor, Works in Progress.
A specter is haunting the world. The specter of extremely dumb economic policies being advanced by smug don't-know-it-all-and-don't-care-tos. It's a bipartisan phenomenon, though expressed differently on different sides: people who don't understand industrial policy architecting the tariff system you'd design if you wanted America to be more reliant on other countries for manufactured goods, rent control and grocery systems set up to make the provision of a given amount of housing and food as expensive and inconvenient as possible, etc.
The desired outcomes are debatable, and, in fact, should be the locus of debate. The fact to remember in all of these discussions is that America is a rich country, and is, in fact, so rich that it can sacrifice gobs of economic growth in order to achieve particular policy aims. But the other fact is that there is a sacrifice involved; policy is about tradeoffs, and to the extent that a fix-everything switch exists, the burden of proof is on the person who wants to flip it.
Central Park would be more valuable if we paved it over and stacked apartments and office buildings on top, but New York is rich enough to afford a nice park; America can be much more restrictive on immigration before it's not the default destination for top global talent. But one of the key beliefs of the anti-slopulist coalition is that "a lot" is not "infinity," that costs add up, and that if you get in the habit of going shopping with a credit card without looking at the price tag, you may find yourself surrounded by junk and buried in debt.
As a political science term, slopulism is in the same category as fascism, where it doesn't describe a coherent political program, but a means of enacting whatever program happens to be favored by people willing and able to use those means. The slopulist approach is to cast an issue not in terms of tradeoffs, but in terms of enemies (friends usually get lower billing): foreign competition, landlords, private equity, Big Tech, etc. There's often a sprinkling of numbers, but a key element of the slopulist argument is that these numbers are not actually inputs into the argument. They're purely decorative, the way medieval monks who copied the Bible by hand would often make the opening of one of the books into a beautiful work of abstract art surrounding a few words. The slopulist approach to statistics is that, just ugly.
A famous example of this from a while back was when the book Empire of AI overestimated the water use of a datacenter compared to a nearby city by literally a thousandfold. The author at first expressed some uncertainty as to whether numbers implying that the average person in a city in Chile consumes about five ounces of water a day might be inaccurate, but later, admirably, issued a correction. However, there's a missing meta-correction: at the start of the chapter, or perhaps of the book, it should have said "this book cites a number of statistics. However, you can vary them by orders of magnitude without changing anything about the argument, so feel free to ignore them." Granted, most readers will ignore them; it took an independent blogger to read the book, notice that the numbers were nonsensical, identify the source of the error, flag it to the author, and persuade her that this made a meaningful difference. But it should make a difference! If you were worried about AI consuming too much water, and someone told you they invented a machine that could eliminate 99.9% of AI's water use, you'd be thrilled! It turns out that in this case, that machine is "an LLM chatbot into which you paste a copy of the government report and ask it whether the units are probably liters or cubic meters of water," but the principle would be the same if the other side had principles.
Tariffs have faded into the background, but it's essential to remember just how slapdash the initial rollout was—a decision so bad that a tweet that misinterpreted an interview as implying that the tariffs were being paused for 90 days led to a $2.4tr intraday rally ($, WSJ). Imagine how bad a job you have to be doing if the rumor that you're going on vacation creates more instantaneous wealth than a surprise rate cut or the announcement of a Covid vaccine.[1]
The reason for this was not just that the market was not especially fond of industrial policy, but that they were worried about bad industrial policy, particularly one that just treated the US' trade deficit with a given country as a measure of how abusive its policies are. It's true that formal trade barriers are not the only way a country can subsidize its exports—pushing its currency down or having informal trade barriers like artificially rigorous quality requirements (in the 70s, the Japanese government required imported boats to pass the "drop test," where they'd be dropped from 2.5 meters into the water and then inspected for damage. Locally-manufactured boats were exempt). But it's also true that trade is global, and that bilateral deficits are a necessarily incomplete picture, especially for small companies whose economies are more specialized for law-of-large-numbers reasons—if your country first industrializes with textiles, the next factory built is a lot more likely than average to make t-shirts and sandals; if it's electronics assembly, the next factory is more likely to make TVs. The US happens to specialize in exports that disproportionately consumed by high-income countries (Boeing planes, Intuitive Surgical robots), or exports of intangibles that show up as wages and corporate profits[2] but lead to a negative trade balance. That's a feature of globalization, where some US supply chains create a trade deficit but also increase the net present value of American profits, such that selling a slice of those profits in order to fund imports is a good deal for both sides. There are plenty of US manufacturers that aren't as big and don't have sales as skewed to high GDP per capita countries, and many of these companies use imported goods as inputs. From the perspective of maintaining a high value-added manufacturing sector, that's ideal: steel can be in many places (including here), but adding value to it in some unique way and then selling the resulting products at home and abroad tends to create more value-add per hour, and a more indispensable manufacturing sector. A good industrial policy does a mix of two things:

Defensively, identifying cases where another country is subsidizing or otherwise protecting a particular industry with the goal of monopolizing it. There's a lot of this in China, partly because the structure of their financial system directly subsidizes industries that meet the state's priorities. But if the US doesn't want its policy on Taiwan, Vietnam, or other neighboring countries to be determined by access to processed rare earth metals, shipping containers, solar-grade wafers, or precursors for antibiotics, it needs to develop other reliable (non-chinese) sources for those.
Offensive industrial policy, identifying industries where the US could have a comparative advantage, particularly at scale, and using the government's immense financial firepower and ability to rewrite rules as a way to achieve that scale. The US is doing a soft version of this in AI, and a more direct one in chips—directly investing in and subsidizing chip companies is an indirect subsidy to AI both because it decreases the cost of inputs and because it implies that the government, or at least the current administration, won't let the AI boom fall apart.

These are both industry-specific, and they require research, and a plan. They stick it to foreign countries more effectively per dollar of deadweight loss than a blanket tariff, so even someone making tariff policy who views the world in a zero-sum way, where making other countries poorer automatically makes America richer, can see that the benefits to a targeted approach are yuge.
Slopulism mostly shows up in national issues, because everyone can have an opinion. Local politics is no escape. Consider NYC's Delivery Protection Act, which would require Amazon to bring drivers onto its payroll rather than outsourcing to third-party contractors. Meanwhile, the Teamsters are doing an organizing drive for Amazon drivers. As Matt Stoller could probably tell you, a monopoly on some kind of valuable service with high fixed costs, like delivering Amazon packages in New York, is ripe for abuse. That's the concern—that Amazon packages in a big city would be delivered by workers who can go on strike collectively rather than one delivery business at a time, and that Amazon will lose less from even a short strike than from raising their pay and then either raising its prices or eating the cost to margins. Let's see how advocates defended it: here's the speaker of the City Council, pointing out that Amazon is "a $3 trillion corporation," and asserting that these changes won't impact prices or jobs. Here's the mayor, who clarifies that it's a multi-trillion dollar corporation, and still run by Jeff Bezos. This is just a really limp argument. Yes, Amazon is worth trillions of dollars, and the cost of this is small compared to Amazon, but Amazon is also composed of many businesses other than delivering packages in New York, not to mention their side business renting out computers. There is no particular reason that someone backing up their data in S3 or ordering an iPhone charger in Phoenix should subsidize cheap Amazon deliveries or, equivalently, higher wages for drivers in one geography.[3]
Amazon's response is, from what I can tell, more slop. They say this could add up to $5 to each order. But Amazon delivery drivers seem to target anywhere from 10-35 stops per hour. At 25 stops an hour, a $5 cost increase would imply that the workers got a $125/hr raise. Even if you assume that they also get less efficient, you have to make pretty extreme assumptions to get to $5.
It would be nice if Amazon were a little more straightforward, and just said: this is a small cost that we'll partly eat and partly pass on to you; the profit-maximizing number of packages to ship into Manhattan will be lower than otherwise, but really not enough to notice. But this is just a way that your taxes are even higher than you think, and with no discernable benefit to you. Meanwhile, it would be refreshing if the New York City Council said that New York City has decided to redistribute some economic output from capital to labor, more specifically organized labor, which is friendly to them. And that if you'd like to be a friend of the mayor in line for these extras, you ought to look into organizing! It'll take some money out of Amazon's pocket. And yes, prices will be a little higher to offset these labor costs. But you'll barely notice that cost, while some workers will definitely notice the benefits.
That's a reasonable discussion to be had! You can argue for benefiting New Yorkers as consumers, New Yorkers as organized laborers, New Yorkers as workers generally, etc. You can sidestep that question entirely by saying that the status quo relies on lots of companies continuously deciding whether or not to deliver for Amazon, and their workers all deciding whether or not to work with them—that multiple delivery companies in the same area means that there are multiple bidders for the exact same set of workers, which makes price discovery for workers unusually straightforward. That everyone involved has easy ways to express dissatisfaction with the system, and they don't take them.
If there's a point that slopulism got big, it was probably during the student loan forgiveness debacle. To recap: no prudent lender is going to give an eighteen-year-old an unsecured five-figure loan on the expectation that they won't have any income for four years and only then will start servicing it by means currently unknown (and increasingly unknowable&mdsah;will we have the same flavor of entry-level white collar or academic work in 2030?). So the government steps in, and provides subsidized loans. These loans are on incredibly generous terms, including not just low interest rates but options to defer payments. Deferral leads to the payments compounding, which apparently surprises many borrowers. So, payments were paused in 2020, and there were attempts with varying degrees of success to partially cancel them.
The underlying problem with all of this is that the function of student loans is at odds with their being structured as a loan. A loan makes sense if every degree is supposed to pay off well financially, and if students are, fundamentally, spending time and tuition on some abstract capex which will subsequently produce returns. But that's not what every kind of education is for. Some things are worth learning, and some disciplines are worth having, even if there isn't direct financial upside—if some of them, like majoring in theology, can branch into career tracks that involve literal vows of poverty. If you must be an accountant about it, you can say that having some people study this kind of thing produces a positive externality. But in that case, the way to fund it is a grant.
If they're mere loans, then it's easier to treat them as just a movement on the balance sheet, converting $1 of cash on hand into $1 of loans. But if they default, someone needs to take the financial hit: the money has already been spent on tuition, and can't be recovered from the school. The ultimate cost of the loan is whatever resources—people and real estate, mostly—were allocated to providing education to someone who wasn't going to pay back their loans. If it's a real loan, that's a real cost; the degree is only collateral if it's expected to produce some cash flow in the future. Which doesn’t necessarily mean it's not worthwhile, just that it should be discussed explicitly as something to subsidize, not to invest in. A flat per-student subsidy for accredited schools would actually accomplish this on the margin, since it has the biggest relative impact on the worst-paying degrees. And paying for this with slightly higher taxes for the last few brackets would mean that basically the same demographic that paid back its student loans would also be the ones paying slightly more back into the system.
But that's pretty boring! It doesn't polarize people the way putting millions of student borrowers on one side and millions of net taxpayers on the other. The pro-loan forgiveness side didn't spend a lot of time talking about the college wage premium, which made loan forgiveness a form of redistribution towards a relatively richer demographic. And there didn't seem to be a lot of urgency to figure out if the supply of higher education was too high relative to the demand. If an argument whose salience rose with people's level of education could support such a superficial discourse, there's no limit.
Slopulism is what it is because it's appealing by default. That makes fighting it an uphill battle. But you can turn that around and make it about status, where being in the majority puts someone on the back foot already. It should be embarrassing to everyone involved to treat these issues so simplistically, and to pretend that the other side is always ignoring the magic have-zero-tradeoffs switch. Which means that anyone who brings up the tradeoff-free argument looks like a yokel when they get the obvious follow-up question. "Compared to what?" "How did you get that number?" and "Are you sure that's true?" are universal solvents for the vast majority of slopulists, which lets slop-avoidant elitists inhabit a trendy gray area instead of insisting on black and white.

Disclosure: long AMZN.

It was no a surprise that there were people working on the vaccine, but the timing did surprise people, because Pfizer had said they expected to know if the vaccine worked by the end of October 2020, while acknowledging that the schedule could slip. Pfizer and BioNTech got a negative sell-side note in late October, because of concerns that these delays implied low efficacy. It worked out, of course, but the closer you were watching vaccine-related news around this time, the more worried you might be that it was herd immunity plus lots of death or nothing. ↩︎

In that order—total wages and benefits in the US are about 4.1x corporate plus LLC profits. ↩︎

It will be harder to look at the outcome of this, if implemented, and definitively measure an impact on prices. Amazon prices products in reference to other products they sell in order to maximize long-term contribution profit per customer, inclusive of money spent on ads. It's a naturally opaque system, where we shouldn't expect to have good intuitions about what this does to the cost of ordering a pair of Crocs or a book. But what we can say is that if there's some extra cost, it gets covered by somebody, and the only case in which Amazon eats all of it is if they're a monopolist charging the profit-maximizing price. ↩︎

Super-Voting Org Charts
As you may have noticed, Nvidia is worth about a trillion dollars more than it was on Friday night, and Nasdaq futures were briefly halted because they rose so fast ($, WSJ), after Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO. Right there in the first paragraph is:

In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

This lines up nicely with Ben Thompson's thesis on the firing: Jensen Huang didn't realize that Nvidia had become a defense contractor (at that point you want to restrict extramarital affairs with potential spies to the Five Eyes, or at a minimum NATO members). At that point, the board's job is partly to provide routine governance, but occasionally to ratify the decisions made by who's actually in charge. And the government is operating under their own constraints: Nvidia is important to the AI trade, which is important to both the stock market and the US's strategic position with respect to China. And Jensen set the company up in a way that makes him hard to remove, especially if that removal is because one faction had a temporary advantage. It's another instance of thermostatic state capacity ($, Diff): they can remove someone they don't like, but they can't remove someone they need.
Sanctions and Supply Chains
The Economist covers some fairly aggressive corporate espionage from China ($), including setting up front companies in Taiwan in order to hire Taiwanese workers, in some cases as simple poaching and in some cases to get whatever intellectual property they walk out the door with. For lower-income and potentially higher-growth countries, industrial espionage has high returns, and in China's case, those returns are higher because they have enough domestic R&D capacity to extend that work further. Which either forces the US to enforce more separation between American- and Chinese-aligned supply chains, and to accept that not only do open-weight models from China tend to catch up to proprietary models from the US, but that over time, hardware constraints can relax and the open/closed gap can shrink.
Liquidity
Oracle says they have access to all the funding they need to meet their OpenAI obligations, and says "we became the first hyperscaler fully funded for this investment cycle." Which is an interesting way to call the top, or at least call a slowdown, in datacenter construction. Oracle has recently shifted a large share of its enterprise value over to what amounts to a neocloud business, which is not something the market favors. But Oracle can market itself as the most blue-chip of the neoclouds, given the size of its other businesses and the fact that it doesn't currently plan to raise more capital. If Oracle's long-term bullish but worried that there's too much capacity entering the market, then the optimal approach for them is to do what they can to make their stock a good currency to acquire distressed competitors.
Targeted Tariffs
The EU has passed rules making it easier to block specific imports or apply tariffs and quotas. One side effect of Donald Trump bringing back tariffs was that other countries started using them. It turns out that tariffs are quite a fun tool for benefiting or harming particular constituencies, which made the gradual decline in US tariffs over most but by no means all of the period since the start of the 20th century. In the short term, they're effective when the goal is to get exactly the negative externality they cause: an increase in the cost of some product that leads to less of it being bought than otherwise. It is possible, though hard, to design a tariff system that does that without penalizing imports you actually want more of.
Political Pull
There's still a bull market in politics on, given how much midterms and national security questions have determined equity prices over the last few weeks. But any bull market has pockets of underperformance, and so it is with Trump's crypto empire, where the cost of a seat has dropped 99% since May 2025. There are many, many downsides to a President actively engaging in business while in office, particularly in a business whose main product is access to Donald Trump in his capacity as President and whose main financial upside goes to Donald Trump in his role as a private citizen. But one perk is that it gives you a live way to mark influence to market. The prospect of getting Trump's attention used to be valuable, even if this means of doing so entailed a reputational hit. Now, it's a budget option for a Florida vacation if a weekend Disney World is out of your price range.
